newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK authority says new airport to absorb growth.
newsitem.headline: HK authority says new airport to absorb growth.

text.p: Hong Kong's Airport Authority, which has proposed raising fees airlines pay when a new airport opens next year, said on Saturday the facility will keep pace with huge growth in regional aviation markets.

"We are building the new airport within the parameters that have been set jointly by the British and Chinese governments," a statement quoted chairman Wong Po-yan as telling the Royal Aeronautical Society in London on Friday.

"These include a requirement that we should maintain Hong Kong's status as a centre of international and regional aviation, and also ensure that the airport business is conducted on prudent commercial principles."
The authority is in charge of developing Chek Lap Kok airport, which is scheduled to open in April 1998, replacing Kai Tak airport.
Britain hands back Hong Kong to China on July 1 this year, after ruling the territory for more than 150 years.

The authority said estimates showed regional airlines would take delivery of 3,400 new commercial aircraft and that about US$200 billion would be spent on airport development in the Asia-Pacific region over the next 20 years.
The 10 international airports currently being built in Asia "indicates how aviation markets are set to grow", it said.

Hong Kong's new airport will have an initial capacity of 35 million passengers a year, rising to 87 million passengers and nine million tonnes of cargo when development is complete, the statement said.
But the airport authority and airlines have been at odds over user charges at the US$20.3 billion facility.

On Friday, the authority said it had proposed nearly doubling the charges airlines currently pay when Chek Lap Kok opens. The charges include landing fees, parking fees and passenger terminal fees, chief executive Henry Townsend told a business luncheon. Townsend said the airport authority would consult with the International Air Transport Association (IATA) on the proposed charges and that more information would be made available at the next meeting of the authority and the airlines in late April.
IATA expressed disappointment after talks held with authority earlier this week.
